problem: Existing human-aware navigation simulators rely on handcrafted pedestrian rules (SFM/ORCA), scripted animations and near-perfect 2D observations, and lack photorealistic rendering, joint-level pedestrian control and GPU-parallel simulation for RL.
motivation: Human-aware navigation needs large-scale, diverse HRI data and fair benchmarks. Implicit visual cues such as body orientation and gait shape human intention, but simulators cannot provide them. Parallel photorealistic simulation would also speed up RL training.
key_idea: Build a benchmark on Isaac Lab that combines photorealistic scenes, GPU-parallel environments and physics-based SMPL pedestrians driven by a trajectory diffusion model (TRACE) plus an AMP whole-body controller (PACE), and use it to train a vision-based RL navigation baseline.
insight: Replacing SFM with the diffusion trajectory generator under the same AMP controller improves pedestrian reliability (success 74.24 to 88.67, agent collisions 17.17 to 7.81), so the high-level trajectory generator matters. The AMP pedestrians cover more AMASS pose modes than Isaac Sim's built-in animations (coverage 0.92 vs 0.34, MMD 0.327 vs 0.771). More parallel robots reduce training time and raise final reward, but throughput scaling becomes sublinear because of the coupled robot-crowd pipeline, not the AMP controller.
method: Scene Construction: USD photorealistic artist-crafted scenes from the OmniGibson dataset (30 scenes across scales), occupancy grids, and A* global paths shared by robots and pedestrians.

Trajectory Generation: a TRACE-style U-Net diffusion model conditioned on past states, neighbor trajectories and an occupancy map outputs 5 s future trajectories that refine sparse waypoints. An SFM interface is also provided.
Whole-body Controller: an AMP goal-conditioned PPO policy on 24-joint SMPL humanoids, trained on 2,848 AMASS clips with reward r = r_amp + 0.5 r_task (tracking, energy, no-backward terms).

Parallel Simulation and Benchmark Suite: multiple scenes spawn simultaneously in Isaac Lab. It provides a Gym interface, Stable-Baselines3 compatibility, RGB-D sensing, the Nova Carter robot and human-aware metrics.
Perception Encoder: Monoloco++ estimates pedestrian body orientation from RGB, and YOLO11 tracking with depth gives velocity. Each agent state is [x,y,u,v,cos/sin θ,radius] over 8 history steps.

Factorized Spatio-Temporal Transformer: 3 blocks of temporal then agent-wise attention, a CNN occupancy-map feature, goal-query cross-attention with a gated update, feeding a PPO policy that outputs (v, ω).
Reward: +20 at goal, -20 on collision, a proximity penalty inside 0.9 m, dense goal-progress shaping, and a penalty on sharp turns.

setting.backbone: Factorized spatio-temporal Transformer + PPO (trained from scratch); Monoloco++ pose/orientation (off-the-shelf); diffusion U-Net + AMP MLP policy for pedestrians
setting.training_data: Pedestrian controller: 2,848 AMASS motion clips. Navigation policy: online RL in NavIsaacLab (station, home, grocery store scenes). No web data.
setting.observation: Egocentric RGB-D (for pedestrian orientation and velocity), occupancy map, goal relative to the robot
setting.action_space: Continuous velocity (v, ω) for a differential-drive base
setting.privileged: none stated; occupancy map and global A* path used as inputs

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark results. The paper reports pedestrian-simulation quality and parallel-throughput numbers (Table 2, Table 3, Fig. parrel) and real-robot qualitative demos; the benchmarking of navigation methods appears only in text and there are no SR/SPL tables.
results: Diffusion+AMP pedestrians beat the SFM+AMP variant (success 88.67 vs 74.24, fall 1.12 vs 4.99, agent collision 7.81 vs 17.17) and are more diverse than Isaac Sim animated people (coverage 0.92 vs 0.34). Parallel robots cut training time and raise reward; human-only throughput rises from 16.7 to 175.3 agent steps/s at 64 pedestrians. The policy transferred to a Scout Mini in a corridor and a lobby without tuning, shown only qualitatively.
limitations: No quantitative benchmark tables comparing navigation methods and no quantitative sim-to-real metrics, despite the benchmark claims.
The AMP controller tracks only 64.6% of clips under a strict criterion, and full robot-crowd throughput scales sublinearly.
Limited to one robot base (Nova Carter) and uniform pedestrian appearance.
